title: Zinc and Copper Labs: Sampling, Zinc-Induced Copper Deficiency and Menkes Disease
summary: Learn why plasma zinc depends on timing, meals and haemolysis, how excess zinc causes copper deficiency, why serum copper and ceruloplasmin are confounded markers, and how Menkes disease (ATP7A) differs from Wilson disease.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 27 Hits 3 (Menkes), 10 (zinc deficiency; zinc excess causes copper deficiency), 12 (ceruloplasmin acute-phase; serum copper insensitive) and Exam Traps 4 (low serum copper) and 6 (zinc sampling). Checked against King 2015 (BOND zinc review; read via a page-fetch tool), Tümer 2010 (read via a page-fetch tool), Jaiser 2010, Wahab 2020, Ganaraja 2025, Monangi 2024 and Iskandar 2005. Nuances: zinc cut-offs depend on fasting, time of day and sex; serum and plasma zinc did not differ when handled alike (the reviewer prefers plasma and says serum runs 5–10% higher; register flag rv-zinc-serum-plasma); low copper and ceruloplasmin are physiologically low in newborns (rv-menkes-neonatal-copper); the reviewer’s erythrocyte SOD activity as the better copper marker is not supported by the one study read (rv-copper-sod-marker). Not taught (pending): “RBC copper normal” in Menkes, “dwarfism”, the acrodermatitis enteropathica cut-off <40 µg/dL. The NIH ODS copper fact sheet and GeneReviews Menkes chapter were blocked (403/captcha) and were not read.

objectives: Explain how time of day, meals, inflammation and haemolysis change plasma zinc, and how to collect a valid sample.
Describe how excess zinc causes copper deficiency and its haematological and neurological effects.
Explain why serum copper and ceruloplasmin can mislead, and distinguish Menkes disease from Wilson disease.

scenes.title: Three trace-metal results
scenes.altText: Invented scenario. Three results: (1) a 62-year-old who uses a lot of denture adhesive, with anaemia, neutropenia and an unsteady gait — serum copper low, serum zinc high; (2) a plasma zinc reported “normal” on a non-fasting afternoon sample with slight haemolysis; (3) a 4-month-old boy with seizures and sparse, pale, wiry hair — serum copper and ceruloplasmin low. Question token: “Which result can you trust, and what does it mean?”

cues.text: Three trace-metal results. A denture-adhesive user with anaemia, low white cells and an unsteady gait has low copper and high zinc.
A zinc level is reported normal, but the sample was taken in the afternoon, after a meal, and is slightly haemolysed.
And a four-month-old boy with seizures and pale, wiry hair has low copper. Which result can you trust, and what does each mean?

scenes.title: Where zinc and copper sit in blood
scenes.altText: Schematic: a blood tube with plasma above cells. Zinc card (King 2015, BOND zinc review): blood cells hold about 10 times the zinc concentration of plasma, so haemolysis falsely raises plasma zinc; plasma zinc is highest in the morning before breakfast, falls for several hours after each meal and can swing by as much as 20% across the day; it also falls with infection and inflammation; albumin is its primary carrier. Copper card (Monangi 2024; Ganaraja 2025): ceruloplasmin carries about 75–95% of circulating copper; ceruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant that rises with infection and inflammation, and because its gene has oestrogen response elements it can rise in pregnancy, with hormone replacement and with some oral contraceptives.

cues.text: Zinc lives mostly inside cells. Blood cells carry about ten times the zinc concentration of plasma, so even a little haemolysis pushes plasma zinc up falsely.
Plasma zinc is highest in the morning before breakfast. It falls for hours after each meal, can swing by up to twenty percent across the day, and drops with infection and inflammation.
Copper in blood rides mainly on ceruloplasmin, which carries roughly seventy-five to ninety-five percent of circulating copper.

Ceruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant: it rises with infection and inflammation, and with oestrogen, in pregnancy, hormone replacement and some oral contraceptives. That can hide a low copper state.

scenes.title: Zinc too low, zinc too high, copper that cannot get in
scenes.altText: Three cards. Zinc deficiency (King 2015): growth retardation, poor appetite, impaired immunity; with more severe deficiency, delayed sexual maturation and hypogonadism in males; also delayed wound healing and taste abnormalities — mostly non-specific. Acrodermatitis enteropathica: an autosomal recessive defect of zinc metabolism; in one series mean plasma zinc was about 38 µg/dL on days with clinical signs. Zinc excess (King 2015; Jaiser 2010; Wahab 2020): very high zinc intake (about ≥50 mg/day) interferes with copper absorption — zinc induces metallothionein in gut cells, copper binds it more tightly than zinc and is lost when the cells slough; sources include denture adhesive cream, supplements, zinc-containing creams and over-supplemented dialysate; result: anaemia, neutropenia and a myelopathy that mimics vitamin B12 subacute combined degeneration. Menkes disease (Tümer 2010): X-linked recessive ATP7A defect; copper export from intestinal cells is defective so absorption is reduced; ATP7A is expressed in almost every organ except the liver, where ATP7B (the Wilson gene) predominates; sparse, lustreless hair from about 1–2 months, with hypopigmented hair that resembles steel wool; seizures from about 2–3 months; regression around 5–6 months; usually diagnosed at 3–6 months; low serum copper and ceruloplasmin support the diagnosis but are also low in healthy newborns.

cues.text: Zinc deficiency slows growth, dulls appetite and immunity, delays sexual maturation, and impairs taste and wound healing. Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal recessive defect of zinc handling, with very low plasma zinc while signs are present.
Too much zinc is also a problem. Above about fifty milligrams a day, zinc switches on metallothionein in gut cells. Copper binds it tightly and is shed with the cells, so copper absorption fails.
Denture creams, supplements and zinc-rich dialysate have all caused this. The result is anaemia, neutropenia, and a spinal cord disease that looks like vitamin B12 deficiency.

Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive defect in ATP7A. Copper cannot leave the gut cells, so the body runs short. Expect seizures from two to three months, then pale, steel-wool hair, with low serum copper and ceruloplasmin.

scenes.title: Reading the three results
scenes.altText: Decision cards. (1) Low copper with high zinc in a denture-adhesive user: fits zinc-induced copper deficiency — ask about denture cream and supplements; stopping the zinc source and giving copper improved the blood counts in a published case. (2) Zinc: suggested lower cut-offs depend on sampling (BOND; µg/dL): morning fasting 70 (females ≥10 y) / 74 (males ≥10 y); morning non-fasting 66 / 70; afternoon 59 / 61. Haemolysis falsely raises the value, so a “normal” haemolysed afternoon result is untrustworthy: recollect in the morning, fasting, with stainless-steel needles and trace-element-free tubes (zinc-free heparin for plasma), without haemolysis. Early studies found serum zinc slightly higher than plasma, but the difference disappeared when both were held equally long before separation. (3) Infant: low copper and ceruloplasmin support Menkes disease, but both are physiologically low in newborns, so interpret with caution; DOPA-to-DHPG catecholamine ratio and ATP7A testing help. Copper card: serum copper and ceruloplasmin are affected by many conditions unrelated to copper intake and are thought to be insensitive to marginal deficiency.

cues.text: Result one: low copper with high zinc in a denture-adhesive user fits zinc-induced copper deficiency. Ask about creams and supplements. In a published case, stopping the zinc and giving copper improved the blood counts.

Result two cannot be trusted. Zinc cut-offs depend on timing: lower in the afternoon, higher in the morning fasting state. Haemolysis pushes zinc up. Recollect in the morning, fasting, in trace-element-free tubes, without haemolysis.
Result three: low copper and ceruloplasmin support Menkes disease, but healthy newborns also have low values, so interpret them with care. Catecholamine ratios and ATP7A testing help.
And remember: serum copper and ceruloplasmin are pushed around by inflammation and oestrogen, and are thought to miss marginal copper deficiency.

props.label: Serum Cu / ceruloplasmin: confounded, miss marginal deficiency

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A normal zinc is normal, whenever it was drawn” (✓ zinc is highest fasting in the morning, falls after meals and in the afternoon, and haemolysis falsely raises it); “A normal serum copper or ceruloplasmin rules out copper deficiency” (✓ ceruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant raised by inflammation and oestrogen, and both markers are thought to miss marginal deficiency); “Menkes, like Wilson, is copper overload” (✓ Menkes is an X-linked ATP7A defect of copper export from gut cells — the body is copper deficient).

cues.text: Trap one: a normal zinc is normal whenever it was drawn. No: timing, meals and haemolysis all change it.
Trap two: a normal copper or ceruloplasmin rules out copper deficiency. No: ceruloplasmin rises with inflammation and oestrogen, and both miss marginal deficiency.
Trap three: Menkes, like Wilson disease, is copper overload. No: in Menkes the body is short of copper because it cannot get out of the gut cells.

props.title: ✗ “Normal copper rules out deficiency.”
lines: ✓ Acute-phase and oestrogen effects; misses marginal

props.title: ✗ “Menkes = copper overload.”
lines: ✓ ATP7A: Cu cannot leave gut cells · deficient

scenes.title: Zinc locks the copper door
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “ZINC LOCKS THE COPPER DOOR: too much zinc makes the gut cell grab copper and throw it away. MENKES: the door out of the gut cell is jammed (ATP7A), so copper never reaches the body. WILSON: the liver’s exit to bile is jammed (ATP7B), so copper piles up.” Tokens: zinc excess → Cu deficient · Menkes = jammed gut exit · Wilson = jammed liver exit. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: zinc locks the copper door. Too much zinc makes gut cells grab copper and throw it away. In Menkes, the exit from the gut cell is jammed, so copper never reaches the body. In Wilson, the liver’s exit to bile is jammed, so copper piles up.

Where it breaks: ATP7A works in most tissues, not only the gut; zinc-induced deficiency depends on dose and duration; and copper blood tests are confounded, so a doorway picture does not tell you how much copper is stored.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Zinc effect depends on dose and time

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Zinc: timing-matched cut-off · no haemolysis”, “Zinc excess → copper deficiency · ceruloplasmin is acute-phase · Menkes = X-linked ATP7A, copper deficient”.

cues.text: Judge zinc against a cut-off that matches the fasting state and time of draw and reject haemolysed samples, remember that excess zinc causes copper deficiency, and read copper results with care because ceruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant and Menkes disease is a copper-deficient, X-linked ATP7A disorder.

props.label: Zn excess → Cu low · ceruloplasmin acute-phase · Menkes = ATP7A

explanation.what: Plain language: most zinc sits inside cells and blood zinc moves with meals and the time of day, so a careless sample can look normal when it is not. Too much zinc stops the gut absorbing copper. Copper in blood rides on ceruloplasmin, a protein that rises with inflammation and oestrogen, so blood copper tests can hide a shortage. In Menkes disease, a baby cannot move copper out of gut cells into the body. Scientific terms: plasma zinc concentration (PZC), diurnal variation, trace-element-free tubes, zinc-free heparin, acrodermatitis enteropathica, metallothionein, hypocupraemia, copper deficiency myelopathy, ceruloplasmin (acute-phase reactant, oestrogen response elements), copper chaperone for SOD1 (CCS), ATP7A, X-linked recessive, steel-wool hair, DOPA:DHPG ratio.
explanation.why: Blood cells hold about 10 times plasma zinc, so haemolysis raises it; meals and inflammation lower it. High zinc induces enterocyte metallothionein, which binds copper preferentially and is shed. Ceruloplasmin carries most circulating copper and is an acute-phase, oestrogen-responsive protein. ATP7A exports copper from cells including the intestinal mucosa; its loss lowers copper absorption.
explanation.measure: BOND suggested lower plasma zinc cut-offs (µg/dL): morning fasting 70 F / 74 M (≥10 y); morning non-fasting 65 (<10 y), 66 F, 70 M; afternoon 57 (<10 y), 59 F, 61 M. Avoid haemolysis and contamination; use trace-element-free tubes. Zinc ≥50 mg/day interferes with copper absorption. Ceruloplasmin carries ~75–95% of circulating copper. Menkes: low serum copper and ceruloplasmin (interpret with caution in newborns); plasma DOPA:DHPG ratio.
explanation.differs: Menkes (X-linked, ATP7A, copper deficient, systemic) vs Wilson (autosomal recessive, ATP7B, hepatic copper overload); zinc deficiency vs zinc excess (which causes copper deficiency); valid fasting morning non-haemolysed zinc vs afternoon, non-fasting or haemolysed zinc.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the cause of anaemia, neutropenia and myelopathy in a denture-cream user; whether a haemolysed afternoon zinc can be reported as normal; why normal ceruloplasmin does not exclude a copper problem; Menkes inheritance, gene and hair.

mnemonic.text: ZINC LOCKS THE COPPER DOOR: too much zinc makes the gut cell grab copper and throw it away. MENKES: the exit from the gut cell is jammed (ATP7A), so copper never reaches the body. WILSON: the liver’s exit to bile is jammed (ATP7B), so copper piles up.

takeaway: Judge zinc against a cut-off that matches the fasting state and time of draw and reject haemolysed samples, remember that excess zinc causes copper deficiency, and read copper results with care because ceruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant and Menkes disease is a copper-deficient, X-linked ATP7A disorder.

questions.stem: A plasma zinc result is within the reference interval, but the sample was drawn in the afternoon after lunch and is slightly haemolysed. What is the best action?

options.text: Request a fasting morning sample collected without haemolysis in a trace-element-free tube
options.rationale: Correct. Zinc is highest fasting in the morning, falls after meals, and haemolysis falsely raises it because cells hold about 10 times plasma zinc.

options.text: Report the result as normal; timing does not affect zinc
options.rationale: Incorrect. Plasma zinc can vary by up to 20% across the day, mainly with meals, and cut-offs differ by timing.

options.text: Report it and add that haemolysis falsely lowers zinc
options.rationale: Incorrect. Haemolysis falsely raises plasma zinc, so a haemolysed “normal” may hide deficiency.

options.text: Repeat the test on the same haemolysed sample
options.rationale: Incorrect. Re-analysis cannot remove the zinc released from the cells; a new, properly collected sample is needed.

questions.stem: A long-term user of large amounts of denture adhesive cream has anaemia, neutropenia and a myelopathy resembling vitamin B12 deficiency. Serum copper is low and serum zinc high. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Zinc induces metallothionein in gut cells, which binds copper and is lost as the cells slough
options.rationale: Correct. This blocks copper absorption and causes zinc-induced copper deficiency.

options.text: Zinc displaces copper from ceruloplasmin into the urine
options.rationale: Incorrect. The mechanism described in the sources is reduced intestinal copper absorption via metallothionein.

options.text: An inherited ATP7B defect prevents biliary copper excretion
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is Wilson disease, which causes copper overload, not low copper from zinc excess.
Incorrect. The myelopathy mimics B12 deficiency but is due to copper deficiency.

questions.stem: Which statement about Menkes disease is correct?

options.text: It is an X-linked recessive ATP7A defect that reduces copper absorption, causing copper deficiency
options.rationale: Correct. Defective copper export from intestinal cells lowers absorption; affected infants are mostly boys.

options.text: It is an autosomal recessive ATP7B defect causing hepatic copper overload
Serum copper and ceruloplasmin are typically high
options.rationale: Incorrect. Both are reduced, although healthy newborns also have low values, so they need careful interpretation.

options.text: Symptoms usually begin in the teenage years
options.rationale: Incorrect. Hair changes can appear at 1–2 months, seizures usually start at about 2–3 months, and most infants are diagnosed at 3–6 months.

claims.text: Cellular zinc ~10× plasma, haemolysis falsely raises zinc; diurnal and meal effects; inflammation lowers zinc; collection precautions; timing-specific cut-offs; serum and plasma zinc did not differ when handled alike.
Signs of zinc deficiency; acrodermatitis enteropathica autosomal recessive with very low plasma zinc during signs.
Zinc excess (≥50 mg/day; denture cream, supplements, dialysate) causes copper deficiency via metallothionein, with anaemia, neutropenia and myelopathy mimicking B12 deficiency.
Ceruloplasmin carries ~75–95% of copper; acute-phase reactant raised by inflammation, pregnancy, hormone replacement and some oral contraceptives.
Serum copper and ceruloplasmin are confounded and thought insensitive to marginal copper deficiency.
Menkes: X-linked recessive ATP7A defect reducing copper absorption; onset, hair, seizures; low copper and ceruloplasmin with neonatal caution; DOPA:DHPG ratio.

Reviewer details not taught: “RBC copper normal” in Menkes; “dwarfism”; acrodermatitis enteropathica cut-off <40 µg/dL; erythrocyte SOD activity as the more meaningful copper marker; serum zinc 5–10% higher than plasma.
claims.note: Not found in, or qualified by, the sources read; see accuracy flags.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 27 Exam Trap 4 says functional tests (erythrocyte Cu-Zn SOD activity) are more meaningful than serum copper. In the one study read (Iskandar 2005, rats), erythrocyte SOD1 activity did not fall significantly in mild zinc-induced copper deficiency, while CCS did; no gold standard exists. The lesson does not teach SOD activity as the better marker (register flag rv-copper-sod-marker).

Ch. 27 Exam Trap 6 says plasma is preferred and the Number Vault says serum runs 5–10% higher than plasma. King 2015 (BOND) reports that early studies found serum zinc slightly higher than plasma, attributed to delayed separation, and that the difference disappeared when handling was matched. BOND cut-offs also differ by fasting state, time of day and sex (register flag rv-zinc-serum-plasma).

Ch. 27 Hit 3 gives low serum copper (RBC copper normal) for Menkes. Tümer 2010 notes low serum copper and ceruloplasmin must be interpreted with caution in newborns because healthy neonates also have low values; “RBC copper normal” was not found in the sources read (register flag rv-menkes-neonatal-copper).
